Jacob parting with his parents, to go to Padan-aram; the charge his father gave him (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.1-Gen.28.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>), the blessing he sent him away with (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.3-Gen.28.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>), his obedience to the orders given him (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.5">ver. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.10">10</reference>), and the influence this had upon Esau, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.6-Gen.28.9">ver. 6-9</reference>. The impression this made upon him, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.16-Gen.28.19">ver. 16-19</reference>. 4. To show the influence of a good example. Esau, though the greater man, now begins to think Jacob the better man, and disdains not to take him for his pattern in this particular instance of marrying with a daughter of Abraham. The elder children should give to the younger an example of tractableness and obedience; it is bad if they do not: but it is some alleviation if they take the example of it from them, as Esau here did from Jacob. Esau did well, but he did it when it was too late, He <hi type="italic">saw that the daughters of Canaan pleased not his father,</hi> and he might have seen that long ago if he had consulted his father's judgment as much as he did his palate. (2.) He took a third wife, while, for aught that appears, his other two were neither dead nor divorced. (3.) He did it only to please his father, not to please God.
